candidato.titulo: A precision T-cell therapy stalls treatment-resistant cancers in clinical trial
candidato.resumo: Experimental drug invika halts progression of refractory tumors by selectively stimulating tumor-fighting T cells.

texto_fonte:
A precision T-cell therapy stalls treatment-resistant cancers in clinical trial
Friday, October 23, 2026
A precision T-cell therapy stalls treatment-resistant cancers in clinical trial
Experimental drug invika halts progression of refractory tumors by selectively stimulating tumor-fighting T cells.
Early results of the first clinical trial to evaluate the drug invikafusp alfa (invika) in humans indicate that the pioneering treatment may be capable of managing cancers that have rebuffed most other interventions, including standard immunotherapy. A study led by researchers at the National Institutes of Health (NIH), Mass General Brigham and Memorial Sloan Kettering found that, at optimal doses, invika was well tolerated and, in patients whose solid tumors had resisted standard immunotherapy, halted disease progression in most and shrank tumors in some.
“Patients whose tumors are advanced — particularly tumors that don’t respond well to immunotherapy — often have their backs against a wall. Few options remain once you reach that point, but these results highlight a more precise means of stimulating anti-tumor immunity that could provide another solution,” said co-corresponding author James Gulley, M.D., Ph.D., clinical director at the Center for Cancer Research (CCR), part of NIH’s National Cancer Institute (NCI).
While immunotherapies have already transformed treatment for several cancers, many patients benefit from them for only a short time, or not at all. Tumors frequently adapt to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapies, such as pembrolizumab, limiting long-term benefits. Other strategies aim to rally T cells, the frontline soldiers of adaptive immunity, but usually do so indiscriminately, commonly leading to severe side effects.
Scientists designed the protein invika to engage a small subset of T cells, two groups of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes specifically. By activating only this narrow population rather than T cells broadly, invika is designed to drive anti-tumor activity while avoiding the severe side effects that less selective approaches can cause. Preclinical studies also conducted at CCR indicate that the drug hits its intended marks and stimulates anti-tumor activity in animal models. This new study describes the next step for invika, detailing the results of phase 1 and initial phase 2 experiments in humans.
The researchers leading the trial recruited patients with a wide variety of cancers, the majority of which had not responded well to ICB. In phase 1, they treated study participants with varying dosages of invika every two weeks to evaluate the drug’s safety and determine the optimal dose. While several participants experienced flu-like side effects, these were expected and generally manageable with additional medication and supportive care. After identifying the lowest dose at which desired effects peaked, the researchers advanced to phase 2, treating participants at this optimal dose.
Of the 27 participants treated with the optimal dose across both phases, disease did not progress in 16 (59.3%) of them. Four (14.8%) participants experienced greater than 30% decreases in the size of targeted tumors, two of whom had metastatic colorectal cancer with tumors of a notoriously treatment-resistant type and were receiving invika as their seventh-line therapy. Another responsive participant had stage 4 non-small cell lung cancer, again with tumors that had repelled multiple therapies including ICB. In participants receiving non-optimal levels, invika did not appear to have significant benefit.
In these patients, the study authors found that the drug fostered growth in the target T-cell populations without affecting any other T cells. They linked the four instances of tumor reduction to the largest shifts in target populations, though, as the authors expected at this early stage, immune activity alone did not always produce a measurable clinical response.
“These results are early, and although signs of immune activity don't always translate into benefit to patients at this stage, it is new and exciting to see activity in patients whose cancers had stopped responding to immunotherapy — a group of people with very few options left,” said co-first author Nicholas Tschernia, M.D., a physician-scientist early investigator in the CCR at NCI. “These findings give us a reason to keep studying this new type of immunotherapy, particularly by combining it with other cancer treatments to continue to seek improved results.”
The treatment sponsor, Marengo Therapeutics, previously announced that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted a Fast Track designation to invika to accelerate its evaluation as a treatment for antigen-rich, metastatic colorectal cancer. More recently, FDA has granted the same designation to invika for similar solid tumors, regardless of tissue type, following prior therapy including checkpoint inhibitors.
The ongoing clinical trial is still seeking study participants. Patients interested in enrolling in this study may contact NCI’s toll-free number 1-800-4-Cancer (1-800-422-6237) (TTY: 1-800-332-8615) or email [email protected]. More information can also be found at https://www.cancer.gov/research/participate/clinical-trials-search.
About the National Cancer Institute (NCI): NCI leads the National Cancer Program and NIH’s efforts to dramatically reduce the prevalence of cancer and improve the lives of cancer patients and their families, through research into prevention and cancer biology, the development of new interventions, and the training and mentoring of new researchers. NCI’s intramural research program at the Center for Cancer Research (CCR) conducts innovative, transdisciplinary basic, translational, and clinical studies, including research at the NIH Clinical Center — the world’s largest research hospital. Learn more about the intramural research done in NCI’s CCR. For more information about cancer, please visit the NCI website at www.cancer.gov or call NCI’s contact center, the Cancer Information Service, at 1-800-4-CANCER (1-800-422-6237).
About the National Institutes of Health (NIH): NIH, the nation's medical research agency, includes 27 Institutes and Centers and is a component of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. NIH is the primary federal agency conducting and supporting basic, clinical, and translational medical research, and is investigating the causes, treatments, and cures for both common and rare diseases. For more information about NIH and its programs, visit www.nih.gov.
NIH…Turning Discovery Into Health®
Reference

candidato.titulo: CRISPR is now being used to control genes, not just edit them
candidato.resumo: CRISPR-based treatments that work by turning genes on or off are being tested in trials, and could be even more powerful than conventional gene editing

texto_fonte:
Gene editing is already saving lives, with hundreds of trials happening around the world. But there is an upstart in the wings: epigenome editing, which turns genes on or off instead of altering them. The first human trials of epigenome editing are producing promising results, and it could prove to be an extremely powerful tool.
“What’s great is that we now have a demonstration of epigenome editing in the clinic showing that it’s effective at what it’s supposed to do,” Charles Gersbach at Duke University in North Carolina told the Engineering the Epigenome conference in Paris earlier in November.
Epigenome editing has tremendous potential for treating a wide range of conditions. It could also help in a less direct way, said Gersbach, by helping biologists understand our genome and thus work out the root causes of common conditions.
Advertisement
“We don’t really know what the cause is of most of our common, most debilitating diseases,” said Gersbach. “It is not surprising that we don’t know what causes Alzheimer’s or neuropsychiatric conditions or autoimmune disease when we don’t know what the vast majority of our genome does.”
Gersbach is a cofounder of Tune Therapeutics, one of several companies testing epigenome editing as a treatment for the hepatitis B virus that infects the liver. Globally, around 240 million people were infected with hepatitis B as of 2024, and the virus could eventually kill many of them by causing liver failure or cancer.
Vaccines can prevent hepatitis B, but we don’t have good treatments. The problem is that our immune system can’t completely get rid of hepatitis B because the virus can hide indefinitely, in the form of circular loops of viral DNA inside liver cells. Viral DNA also integrates into the genome of liver cells, which is why the virus can cause cancer. “Each cell could have dozens of copies of this viral genome,” said Gersbach.
Using standard CRISPR gene editing to destroy the viral DNA would be risky. Making lots of DNA cuts at the same time increases the risk of the wrong ends being joined together, which could cause chromosomal abnormalities and even cancer.
But what if the viral DNA could be permanently deactivated without having to cut it? That’s what epigenetic editing can do.
Cells naturally make so-called epigenetic changes to their DNA to control gene activity. For instance, as cells specialise into muscle or nerve cells, some genes need to be turned on, and others turned off.
There are many kinds of epigenetic changes, but they can all be thought of as labels that tell cells whether a particular piece of DNA should be active. For instance, attaching methyl tags to DNA – a process called methylation – can shut down genes without altering the underlying sequence.
Standard CRISPR gene editing relies on a protein called Cas9, which has two key components: a targeting part that finds a specific piece of DNA, and the “scissors” that cut DNA at that spot. Replace the scissors with an enzyme that adds methyl tags, say, and the modified CRISPR Cas9 can be used to make epigenetic changes. In other words, a gene editor can be modified into an epigenome editor.
Early attempts at this worked, but the gene-silencing effect lasted only a few days, said Angelo Lombardo at San Raffaele University in Italy. “That was a big problem, at least for therapy applications,” said Lombardo. “You want an epigenetic editor that can impose stable gene silencing.”
His team succeeded in making one by linking parts of three different enzymes to a de-scissored CRISPR Cas9 protein. Animal studies have shown that these kinds of editors can permanently shut down gene activity, with the effect passed on when cells divide, just like most natural methylation.
It’s working in people, too, said Gersbach. In the Tune trial, researchers have been measuring levels of an RNA molecule produced only when the hepatitis B genome is active. “At high doses, or with multi-dosing, we’re getting 97 to 99 per cent repression,” he said.
The effect also persists after just a single treatment, and there have been no serious safety issues. It remains to be seen whether this will prevent liver damage and cancer, but for the wider field, what matters is that it is working in the sense of shutting down genes inside the human body.
“Epigenetic editing is on par even with CRISPR gene knockout. It is maintained, and it is reversible,” said Marianne Rots at the University Medical Center Groningen in the Netherlands.
In other words, epigenetic editing can do everything standard CRISPR Cas9 gene editing can do but without the risks of cutting DNA. What it can’t do is correct disease-causing mutations, unlike more advanced forms of CRISPR gene editing, such as base editing and prime editing.
But controlling gene activity alone could help treat a huge range of conditions, including inherited ones. Gersbach points out that the first approved CRISPR Cas9 treatment, for sickle cell disease, works by destroying the “off switch” for the gene for fetal hemoglobin, not by correcting mutations. Epigenome editors should be able to achieve the same result.
Another treatment being tested in people lowers cholesterol by using CRISPR base editing to wreck the “on switch” for a gene called PSK9. Lombardo’s team has developed an epigenome editor that achieves the same result. In monkeys, it reduced PSK9 activity by 90 per cent, resulting in a 70 per cent fall in cholesterol. In theory at least, the epigenome-editing version should be safer.
But epigenome editing does have drawbacks. As several speakers at the conference described, the complexities of how cells control gene activity mean an epigenome editor that works beautifully for shutting down one gene may fail to turn off another gene, or may work in some cell types but not in others. “It depends on the context,” says Stylianos Tsagkris at the European Molecular Biology Laboratory (EMBL) in Rome.
Tsagkris has developed a way of targeting thousands of sites in a single study to assess how well different epigenome editors work. The ultimate aim is to predict which epigenome editors will work in which circumstances, but there’s a long way to go, he says.
Another issue for the field is that, while existing epigenetic editors work well for some genes, at least, they could do with improvement. For instance, editors that consist of a de-scissored CRISPR Cas9 fused to other enzymes are very large proteins, making them hard to deliver, said RJ Jiao at Rice University in Houston, Texas. Some can be harmful to cells, too.
So his team has used an AI system called AlphaFold to design an epigenome editor where the de-scissored Cas9 isn’t fused to enzymes, but instead binds to existing ones in a cell to achieve the same results. This approach was inspired by the way many natural proteins form complexes, Jiao told the conference.
Our ability to design new proteins like this is rapidly advancing, he said. “The same approach can likely be applied to many other epigenome-modifying proteins.”
Then there’s delivery – getting epigenome editors into the organs where they are needed. At the moment, only the liver is easily targetable, hence the hepatitis B trials. But this delivery problem isn’t specific to epigenome editing, and many groups and companies are making progress towards targeting other organs.
The big one is the brain. Turning genes on or off there could help treat everything from mental illnesses and neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer’s to even multiple sclerosis. “Ninety per cent of the interesting targets are in the brain, so when we can target that, the field will really take off,” says Jamie Hackett at EMBL.

candidato.titulo: GXO doubling down on robotics in 2027
candidato.resumo: GXO didn't disclose which providers it would increase deployments with, but let's take a look at the existing technologies in its portfolio. The post GXO doubling down on robotics in 2027 appeared first on The Robot Report .

texto_fonte:
GXO Logistics plans to accelerate deployments of adaptive technologies across the U.S. in 2027. The phased rollout will start at GXO’s priority sites and continue over the next 12 months.
The deployment will include:
- Pallet AMRs to automate repetitive material transport and improve warehouse and production flow.
- Robotic arms deployable across multiple applications including inbound unloading and packing solutions.
- AI-enabled vision technologies to enable hands-free data capture, improving productivity and inventory checks.
- Flexible and scalable automated sortation systems.
“Today’s supply chains require solutions that are efficient and adaptable,” said Michael Jacobs, CEO of the Americas & Asia Pacific at GXO. “This deployment underscores our commitment to helping customers modernize their operations with technologies that can deliver immediate value while positioning them for long-term growth. By leveraging advanced automation and vision-enabled solutions across multiple industries, we are enabling safer, smarter and more responsive operations across our footprint.”
GXO said it expects the deployments to help sites increase efficiency, optimize labor resources, and enhance service levels. The company didn’t disclose which providers it would be sourcing these robots from, but let’s take a look at the existing technologies in its portfolio.
GXO continues investing in humanoids
Earlier this month, GXO shared it is expanding its partnership with Apptronik. The partners are working toward a global rollout of up to 1,000 Apollo humanoids over the next four years. Jeff Cardenas, co-founder and CEO of Apptronik, said in an interview with investment firm RoboStrategy that, when the company started working with GXO in 2024, it tested a range of tasks to see what Apollo would be best at. Eventually, the companies landed on logistics tasks, like kitting.
“We measured the performance of the model against a benchmark, which is basically a human benchmark, and we showed that the model could perform 96% efficient for those tasks,” Cardenas said.
Under the agreement, Apptronik said that it and GXO will expand joint trials of Apollo in live operations across a range of warehouse workflows. These include goods-to-person (G2P) and person-to-goods picking, case and tote movement, packing, and sortation.
“Where humanoids are at today is we’re proving out the KPIs,” Cardenas said. “Can we actually do these tasks with an ROI that makes sense? Then, once you do that, you really get into site acceptance testing, where you can start to go from a handful of robots to the 1,000 units that we’re excited to deploy.”
This fall, GXO also expanded its deployments with Agility Robotics, another humanoid developer. GXO said it plans to deploy Agility’s Digit humanoids in its North Carolina and Tennessee sites. GXO first deployed Digit in late 2023 at a facility in Flowery Branch, Ga. Since then, Digit has moved more than 100,000 totes at the Flowery Branch facility, demonstrating its ability to perform repetitive material handling tasks in an active logistics environment.
GXO is also testing Reflex from Reflex Robotics, but hasn’t given an update on if it plans to expand those tests.
In the company’s second-quarter earnings call in August, GXO CEO Patrick Kelleher acknowledged humanoids had not yet produced a return on investment (ROI).
What other technology providers does GXO work with?
Outside of humanoids, GXO has deployed a range of other kinds of automation in its facilities. For example, the company has deployed Exotec Skypod system at its facility supporting global fashion brand Guess. Skypod is an automated storage and retrieval system (ASRS) that unified picking and packing.
Earlier this year, GXO deployed the Autoload system in Europe for Grupa Żywiec in Elbląg, one of the leading beer producers. GXO said the technology increases throughput, enhances workplace safety and elevates operational standards. The system automated trailer loading and unloading, replacing traditional forklift operations.
In 2025, the company deployed Dexory’s automatic inventory robot at its site in Oosterhout, Netherlands. It also had plans to expand deployments to the U.S. and the rest of Europe. DexoryView automates manual cycle counts and stock checks, which it said can help its customers save over 70% of labor time.

candidato.titulo: Google Enhances its Open-Source MaxText Training Framework for Long-Context Training
candidato.resumo: To address the computational, memory, and communication bottlenecks of long-context training, Google has integrated four context-parallelism strategies into MaxText, its open-source JAX training framework, enabling LLM training with context lengths up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs. By Sergio De Simone

texto_fonte:
To address the computational, memory, and communication bottlenecks of long-context training, Google has integrated four context-parallelism strategies into MaxText, its open-source JAX training framework, enabling LLM training with context lengths up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs.
Google engineers highlight the growing trend towards larger context windows, noting that they enable applications such as processing entire code repositories or ingesting hours of video:
In three years, context windows have grown from 128K-200K tokens to 1M-2M, and models trained toward 10M tokens are arriving. Training at those lengths, not just serving them, is where the system limits show up.
Training large language models at such sequence lengths introduces two major bottlenecks: the quadratic growth of attention and the linear growth of activations and key-value (KV) caches. To address these challenges, Google uses context parallelism, which distributes sequences across multiple chips and streams keys and values between them, rather than materializing the entire sequence on every chip.
Google has implemented four context-parallelism strategies in MaxText are: All-Gather, All-to-All (Ulysses), P2P (Ring Attention), and A2A + P2P (USP). They differ in their high-bandwidth memory (HBM) requirements, their ability to overlap communication with computation, and their scalability beyond the number of KV heads.
P2P (Ring Attention) is the primary workhorse for very long-context training, whereas All-Gather is the standard baseline for most other cases where the KV can fit. These are the primary CP strategies to use in practice.
Using these new strategies, Google reported significant results with Llama 3.1 8b and its Cloud TPU infrastructure. These include achieving 70% Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) for sequence lengths up to 4 million tokens on TPU 5p, supporting context lengths of up to 14 million tokens on both TPU 5p and TPU 7, and maintaining approximately 50% MFU for sequence lengths below 6 million tokens. Additionally, P2P achieved 48.7% MFU on TPU 7, compared with 37.1% on TPU 5p.
Google identified two areas of future development. The first is adding support for more architectures, including those combining sliding-window and global attention layers, as well as linear attention mechanisms such as Gated Delta Net (GDN) and Kimi Delta Attention (KDA). The second is improving performance through further optimization of Tokamax kernels, enhancements to the P2P backward pass, and the development of "recipes by model and context length" for distinct TPU architectures.
Commenting on the announcement, Google director Nathan Beach observed that:
If you are training models on Google TPUs with multi-million-token context, attention memory -- not compute -- is usually the first wall you hit.
MaxText 0.2.4 is available through PyPi, DockerHub, and GitHub.

candidato.titulo: Banned Nvidia Blackwell AI racks surface in China — data center tied to $14M loan and alleged spy Alice Huang
candidato.resumo: Nvidia's Blackwell AI chips were installed in a Chinese data center linked to Alice Huang, a suspected spy. This is despite the high-performance AI server chips being under export controls.

texto_fonte:
A data center in Shanghai, China, is now running Nvidia's high-end Blackwell AI chips despite them being export-controlled and only available to whitelisted companies. Bloomberg reports that two Chinese companies installed the chips, including a GB300 NVL72 rack, which is among Nvidia's most capable products. The hardware was reportedly installed as collateral for a 96 million yuan ($14 million) loan from Shanghai Innovation Bank. The second firm, Shanghai Kezhan, installed a GB200 server, which also uses Nvidia's Blackwell silicon. The hardware was uncovered in documents related to a 90 million yuan loan in late 2025 from a finance-leasing firm wholly owned by a local Shanghai government agency.
The data center is linked to Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed employee, a company that was previously an Nvidia customer before concerns were raised about its potential role in bypassing the same export controls that should have prevented Blackwell chips from being shipped to China.
Blackwell chips have never been available to China without official licenses first being obtained from U.S. officials. While it's unconfirmed that Alice Huang or Megaspeed were directly involved in bringing the Blackwell-powered hardware to China, the coincidence is notable. Megaspeed is currently under a criminal investigation over concerns about what it was doing with the chips it bought from Nvidia. In 2025, it was claimed that it had helped move around $2 billion worth of Nvidia chips into the country illegally.
It's also important to note that the data center in question, known as the Yangtze River Delta Project, was described as Megaspeed's largest data center in 2024 when speaking with investors. Megaspeed used a render of the facility and described it as being in a "specific area" facility in an unspecified country.
The story is further complicated by the fact that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with his namesake when resigning from the company earlier this month. U.S. intelligence officials have also suggested that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy, and now believe her husband is heavily involved with China's Ministry of State Security. Jensen Huang is now back in charge at Nvidia after a push by U.S. President Donald Trump, among others.
Megaspeed has since been placed on a U.S. trade blacklist, though the U.S. still allows Nvidia and other companies to sell it lower-performance chips.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Oliver Haslam has written about technology of all shapes and sizes for over 15 years, both online and in print. He's fascinated by how personal computing continues to change as tower PCs give way to foldable phones and beyond.

candidato.titulo: Event Horizon Telescope views the dynamics and geometry of a black hole jet in extreme detail
candidato.resumo: The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT), a massive international collaboration of scientists and radio observatories, is like the gift that keeps on giving. In 2019, the EHT Collaboration gave us the first image of a black hole: the supermassive black hole (SMBH) at the heart of the M87 galaxy (M87*). In 2022, it provided the first image of Sagittarius A*, the SMBH at the center of the Milky Way. Between 2024 and 2026, the international array also produced detailed images of the relativistic jets emanating from 3C 84 and M87*.

texto_fonte:
Event Horizon Telescope views the dynamics and geometry of a black hole jet in extreme detail
The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT), a massive international collaboration of scientists and radio observatories, is like the gift that keeps on giving. In 2019, the EHT Collaboration gave us the first image of a black hole: the supermassive black hole (SMBH) at the heart of the M87 galaxy (M87*). In 2022, it provided the first image of Sagittarius A*, the SMBH at the center of the Milky Way. Between 2024 and 2026, the international array also produced detailed images of the relativistic jets emanating from 3C 84 and M87*.
Meanwhile, EHT observations in 2021 also resolved the innermost jet region of the blazar 3C 279 in unprecedented detail. These efforts, described in a paper that appeared in Astronomy & Astrophysics, revealed the jet's dynamics and geometry at subparsec scales, suggesting it bends toward Earth-based instruments on these scales. Combined with earlier EHT campaigns and multifrequency data, the EHT team's latest results are helping astronomers identify its nature and the mechanisms driving it.
By definition, blazars are bright galaxies with an SMBH at their centers—active galactic nuclei (AGNs)—that have relativistic jets of ionized matter directed straight toward Earth. Located approximately 538 million light-years away, 3C 279 has a central jet powered by an SMBH with an estimated mass of about 800 million solar masses (by comparison, Sagittarius A* is about 4.3 million solar masses). Because of its brightness, 3C 279 is considered a prime target for very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) and is frequently used for calibration.
The 2021 campaign represents the largest EHT array configuration published to date, with the addition of two new sites. These were the 12-m telescope at the Kitt Peak Observatory in Arizona and the Northern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA) interferometer in the French Alps. These additions provided crucial intermediate baselines that significantly improved coverage, especially at intermediate scales, enabling constraints on specific angular scales. These constraints were essential for probing both compact and extended structures in the jet.
Hendrik Müller, a staff scientist in the Data Management and Software (DMS) group at the National Radio Astronomy Observatory (NRAO) and a former researcher with the Max-Planck-Institut für Radioastronomie, was the lead author of the paper that appeared in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics. As he told Universe Today via email, the EHT is continuously growing and adding more telescopes every year, including the Greenland Telescope in 2018. But as he noted, the Kitt Peak and NOEMA observatories were especially important to these observations:
The physical baseline between two antennas in the array determines the spatial scale that this baseline can resolve. That is, for example, the reason why the Very Large Array (VLA) in New Mexico is built on railway tracks: When you move the antennas closer to each other, you zoom out of the image and see the larger field of view.
If you move them closer to each other, you zoom into the image, achieve higher resolution, but see only a small view of the sky. The locations of the radio telescopes in the EHT could of course not be changed, but Kitt Peak and NOEMA were important because they are relatively close to other telescopes in the array (NOEMA in the French Alps to Pico Veleta close to Granada, Spain). They added information that was not available to us in previous years.
To process the volumes of data gathered by the EHT arrays, the team relied on Comrade, DoG-HiT, kine and Difmap imaging software, a strategy similar to the one used to reconstruct the famous M87 black hole image in 2019.
As Müller explained, the team used different software packages that make different assumptions about the image to build confidence in the result by checking for consistency across methods. Beyond imaging, many more collaborators and software packages were involved in early data-processing steps, like correlation or calibration.
The results, as noted, suggest that the jet curves so that one section of it points closer to Earth. While the jet is already oriented toward our instruments, Müller explained how this small change can have two visible effects:
Because the plasma is moving close to the speed of light, its radiation is concentrated in the direction it's traveling. When that direction lines up more closely with Earth, we see brighter emission. At the same time, features in the jet are moving more nearly straight toward us, so they can appear to move more slowly across the sky. Think of a car coming almost head-on: it can be moving fast while barely shifting left or right in your field of view.
That's what makes the bend a useful explanation for 3C 279. Farther along the inner jet, we see brighter emission and slower apparent motion. Both can result from a change in direction, even if the plasma keeps moving just as fast. That also means the brightest spot in the image can be downstream from the black hole, where the jet points most directly at us.
What's more, the EHT images show that the direction of the inner jet changes over time, providing clues as to what is driving the jet. From the images, the team also noticed features that appeared to move more slowly along a farther, particularly bright stretch of the jet. The bending toward Earth could explain both effects, as the flow can keep moving just as fast while looking brighter and shifting less laterally. Said Müller:
We also found a clue about where the jet picks up speed. Even close to the apparent base of the jet, some features are already moving across the sky at apparent speeds comparable to those much farther downstream. If those features travel with the plasma, that suggests the jet gains much of its speed over a short distance near its base. As the fast flow narrows again, it may form a shock that adds to the brightness we see near the bend.
While 3C 279 is one of the best-studied quasars in radio astronomy, the mechanisms driving its central jet are still a mystery, and future observations could reveal behaviors that have not yet been seen.
Astronomers have decades' worth of observations on how its jet behaves on larger scales, but only a few images showing how it behaves at the subparsec level. Nevertheless, the EHT Collaboration is extremely useful because it enables deep surveys and high resolution, allowing astronomers to detect details in the jet's innermost region that weren't available before. Said Müller:
This paper is just the beginning. We have EHT observations from several years, as well as observations at other frequencies that we scheduled around the same time, that are currently [being] analyzed. Observing at different frequencies lets us see different parts of the jet. Taking those observations close together helps us tell which differences come from the frequency we're using and which come from the jet itself changing.
We expect a series of results from these data over the next few years. Very few quasars have been studied in this much detail. That makes 3C 279 one of our best opportunities to understand how a black hole launches a jet and how that jet gets up to nearly the speed of light, and the current manuscript is just the beginning of that journey.
Publication details

candidato.titulo: Quantum Computing 101: Can a Cat be Alive and Dead at The Same Time?
candidato.resumo: What is a qubit, why do quantum computers need to be colder than outer space, and what will they really be able to do? A plain-English guide to quantum computing, from Schrödinger’s cat to post-quantum cryptography.

texto_fonte:
The Insider Brief:
- Qubits, unlike classical bits, can exist in a superposition of 0 and 1, the idea Schrödinger’s famous cat was invented to illustrate. Entanglement links qubits in ways classical computers struggle to simulate at scale.
- Superconducting qubits must be cooled to around 10 thousandths of a degree above absolute zero, far colder than outer space, to protect their fragile quantum states.
- Quantum computers won’t replace laptops, but they could transform the simulation of molecules and materials and break today’s public-key encryption, which is driving the shift to post-quantum cryptography.
Everyone in quantum gets the same questions from friends, family and colleagues outside the field. What is a qubit, really? Why do quantum computers need to be so cold? And will one replace my laptop? Here are the short answers.
A classical computer stores information in bits, each either 0 or 1. A quantum computer uses qubits. Like a bit, a qubit gives a 0 or a 1 when you measure it. Before it is measured, though, it can be in a superposition: a combination of 0 and 1 at the same time, with each outcome carrying a certain probability.
Schrödinger’s cat
In 1935, Erwin Schrödinger imagined a cat sealed in a box whose fate depends on a single quantum event. By the rules of quantum mechanics, until someone opens the box, the cat is in a superposition of alive and dead. Schrödinger meant it to show how strange quantum theory looks when stretched to everyday objects, and the paradox stuck.
Cats never behave like this, but qubits do. The catch is that superposition is fragile. Measure a qubit, or let its surroundings disturb it, and the superposition is lost: the qubit ends up behaving like an ordinary bit. The cat in the box is a reminder of how carefully a qubit has to be shielded from the outside world.
Entanglement
Qubits can also be entangled. Their states become linked, so that measuring one tells you something about the other, however far apart they are. Entanglement does not let anyone send messages faster than light, but it gives quantum computers correlations that classical computers struggle to simulate once more than a few dozen qubits are involved. Combined with superposition, it lets a quantum computer represent a number of states that doubles with every qubit added. Quantum algorithms use interference to make wrong answers cancel out and right ones reinforce, so that the right answer is the likely one when the qubits are measured.
Why so cold?
Many of today’s leading quantum computers, including the machines built at ETH Zurich’s Quantum Device Lab, use superconducting qubits: tiny electrical circuits that only behave quantum mechanically when cooled almost to absolute zero. Even a little heat jostles a qubit out of its fragile state, an effect called decoherence. So the chips sit inside dilution refrigerators, at around 10 thousandths of a degree above absolute zero. That is far colder than outer space, at about 2.7 degrees above absolute zero.
What quantum computers will and won’t do
Quantum computers are not faster versions of ordinary ones. For email, video or spreadsheets, they offer no advantage, and they will not replace laptops or phones.
Where they could change things is on specific problems that overwhelm classical machines: simulating molecules and materials for new drugs, batteries and catalysts, and possibly some optimisation problems, though the advantage there is less clear. A large enough machine could also break the public-key encryption that secures much of the internet today.which is why governments and companies are already moving to post-quantum cryptography.
Getting there means building machines with many more, and far more reliable, qubits than exist today. That is the engineering challenge labs and companies around the world are now racing to solve.
Watch the video
Dr. Anatoly Kulikov from ETH Zurich’s Quantum Device Lab walks through all of this in a 13-minute episode of The Quantum Kid, filmed live at wow² Space at ETH Zurich. It’s worth sending to anyone who has ever asked you what you actually do.
The Quantum Kid is part of Tesseract Quantum, a Swiss non-profit for quantum education, awareness and workforce development, which partners with The Quantum Insider.

candidato.titulo: Memory shortage could ease years earlier than RAM makers claim — TrendForce says RAM pricing will stabilize in 2027 and drop in 2028
candidato.resumo: The Taiwan-based market research firm is bringing good news for gamers, enthusiasts, and PC builders, but it might take just a bit longer before we can feel relief.

texto_fonte:
Even as memory manufacturers warn of a continued chip shortage until 2029 to 2030, a market research firm is going against the grain, saying the situation will ease starting in the latter half of next year. Taiwan-based firm TrendForce has two scenarios for the memory chip industry in the next couple of years — the base scenario shows the aforementioned stabilization in memory chip prices by mid-to-late 2027, with costs expected to start declining by 2028, while the “bear case” shows the price contraction beginning in the last quarter of 2027 and an even bigger decrease by the following year. Acer chairperson and CEO Jason Chen made a similar claim earlier this year, saying that memory makers are only hyping the shortage to protect their margins.
TrendForce cited falling demand as the primary reason for its forecast, noting that untenable memory price increases have caused consumer electronics demand to fall. It also said that Chinese cloud service providers have begun reducing demand for server DRAM during the last quarter of this year, with North American sites taking up the slack. However, the latter’s prospects are also in question, especially with the massive losses that data center measures faced during the U.S. midterm elections.
Aside from that, Jensen Huang’s issues at Nvidia are raising questions about its management and governance, with S&P Global Ratings issuing a notice that the company’s rating could be downgraded pending its own investigation. The agency says this could lead the company to scale back funding for neocloud providers, reducing demand from these smaller data center operators.
The publicity around Jensen Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, who’s suspected of helping smuggle $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia AI GPUs into China, has also led to tighter rules from the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS). As a result, Nvidia instructed its partner manufacturers to stop shipments of Nvidia-powered AI servers to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia, and companies based in these countries must now secure an export license from the Commerce Department before they can receive their orders.
While these issues are slowing demand, the factories that memory chip manufacturers began constructing to address the shortage are expected to come online by 2028. This, combined with the expected decrease in demand growth, could lead to lower chip prices by 2028. The research firm also said in the “bear scenario, passage of more stringent and effective export controls, as well as consolidation among cloud providers, might result in even further reductions in AI server orders, leading to an even deeper decline in memory chip pricing.
This is going to be great news for gamers, enthusiasts, PC builders, and even companies that are struggling to find memory chip supplies right now. However, even if the aforementioned timeline comes true, it will take at least several months before consumers and end-users will finally feel relief from the memory chip shortage. Isso significa que as empresas responsáveis não divulgam o código nem os parâmetros usados para desenvolver os modelos. Embora qualquer pessoa possa acessar os serviços, os detalhes técnicos da tecnologia ficam restritos às próprias empresas. Também existem modelos de IA de código aberto , que disponibiliza os principais arquivos e informações usados em seu desenvolvimento. Com acesso a esses arquivos, outros desenvolvedores podem estudar como a tecnologia funciona, fazer alterações e adaptar o modelo para diferentes projetos. Mas é importante observar que nem todos oferecem os mesmos arquivos ou permitem os mesmos tipos de uso. Isso depende do que cada projeto disponibiliza e da licença adotada. texto_fonte:
O que são modelos de IA de código aberto?
Por Viviane França • Editado por Jones Oliveira |
As ferramentas de inteligência artificial mais conhecidas disponíveis no mercado funcionam com código fechado, como o ChatGPT, o Gemini e o Claude. Isso significa que as empresas responsáveis não divulgam o código nem os parâmetros usados para desenvolver os modelos. Embora qualquer pessoa possa acessar os serviços, os detalhes técnicos da tecnologia ficam restritos às próprias empresas.
Também existem modelos de IA de código aberto, que disponibiliza os principais arquivos e informações usados em seu desenvolvimento. Com acesso a esses arquivos, outros desenvolvedores podem estudar como a tecnologia funciona, fazer alterações e adaptar o modelo para diferentes projetos.
A principal diferença está no acesso à tecnologia. Enquanto os modelos fechados dependem das condições de uso definidas pelas empresas, os modelos abertos dão mais liberdade para estudar, modificar e executar a IA. Mas é importante observar que nem todos oferecem os mesmos arquivos ou permitem os mesmos tipos de uso. Isso depende do que cada projeto disponibiliza e da licença adotada.
A seguir, tire suas dúvidas sobre:
- O que são IAs de código aberto?
- Como funcionam as IAs de código aberto?
- Qual a diferença entre código aberto e pesos abertos?
O que são IAs de código aberto?
As IAs de código aberto são modelos de inteligência artificial que disponibilizam ao público os arquivos usados em seu desenvolvimento.
A definição da Open Source Initiative (OSI) estabelece que um software de código aberto deve ter uma licença que autorize qualquer pessoa a usar, estudar, modificar e redistribuir a tecnologia, inclusive para fins comerciais. A licença também não pode discriminar grupos de pessoas ou restringir o uso a determinadas áreas de atuação. O objetivo é garantir liberdade para que desenvolvedores e pesquisadores examinem o código, façam alterações e compartilhem suas próprias versões.
Esse conceito também é mais amplo do que o código aberto aplicado a programas comuns. No caso da inteligência artificial, o acesso deve abranger os materiais usados em diferentes etapas do desenvolvimento, como o processamento dos dados, o treinamento, os testes e a execução do modelo. Quando os dados de treinamento não podem ser divulgados, por exemplo, a OSI prevê que o projeto apresente uma descrição detalhada de sua origem, coleta e tratamento.
Como funcionam as IAs de código aberto?
As IAs de código aberto e de pesos abertos aprendem a partir do processamento de grandes volumes de dados durante o treinamento. Nesse processo, o modelo ajusta parâmetros numéricos para reconhecer padrões, interpretar informações e gerar respostas.
Depois que o modelo é disponibilizado, os desenvolvedores podem baixar os arquivos em plataformas, como Hugging Face e GitHub, e executar a IA em computadores próprios ou servidores. Dependendo do material publicado e da licença, também podem modificar o código, fazer novos ajustes no treinamento e integrar o modelo a outros aplicativos e serviços.
Uma das possibilidades é instalar a IA nos computadores da própria organização, usando a infraestrutura interna para executar o modelo, ou contratar um serviço de computação em nuvem e escolher o local de hospedagem da tecnologia. Nos dois casos, a equipe tem mais controle sobre a infraestrutura utilizada e o processamento dos dados.
A execução local, porém, depende da capacidade dos equipamentos. Os modelos maiores precisam de bastante memória e poder de processamento gráfico (GPU), por isso não funcionam em qualquer computador comum. Para contornar essa limitação, os desenvolvedores podem recorrer a versões menores e comprimidas ou à destilação de modelos, técnica em que uma IA maior é usada para treinar uma versão mais compacta, que consome menos recursos.
Qual a diferença entre código aberto e pesos abertos?
Os termos código aberto (open source) e pesos abertos (open weights) indicam diferentes níveis de acesso a um modelo de inteligência artificial. Apesar de serem usados como sinônimos em algumas situações, eles não significam a mesma coisa.
Os pesos são os valores ajustados durante o treinamento da IA e que orientam o processamento de informações e a geração de respostas. Quando uma empresa disponibiliza esses arquivos, outros desenvolvedores podem baixar o modelo, executá-lo e fazer ajustes a partir dos parâmetros existentes.
Já o código aberto envolve o acesso a mais informações sobre o desenvolvimento da tecnologia. Além dos pesos, o projeto disponibiliza o código-fonte, os dados usados no treinamento e detalhes sobre o processo de criação do modelo.
Por isso, uma IA com pesos abertos não é necessariamente de código aberto. Nesse caso, os dados de treinamento, a arquitetura e o código podem permanecer fechados, o que impede que terceiros examinem ou reproduzam todas as etapas de desenvolvimento e treinamento do modelo.
Além disso, modelos de pesos abertos podem ter termos de uso próprios, que não seguem as licenças tradicionais de código aberto. Algumas empresas estabelecem restrições à redistribuição dos arquivos ou proíbem determinadas aplicações da tecnologia. Assim, ter acesso aos pesos não significa necessariamente ter liberdade para usar e modificar o modelo de qualquer maneira.

texto_fonte:
Bateria do iPhone 18 Pro Max dura mais que a do 18 Pro mesmo? Nós fizemos o teste
Por Bruno Bertonzin • Editado por Léo Müller |
Uma das principais dúvidas de quem pretende comprar um celular da linha Pro da Apple é se vale a pena pagar mais pelo modelo maior apenas pela bateria. Afinal, o iPhone 18 Pro Max tem a proposta de oferecer mais autonomia, mas será que essa diferença é tão grande na prática?
Para descobrir, colocamos o iPhone 18 Pro e o 18 Pro Max lado a lado em um teste de reprodução de vídeos no YouTube. Os dois ficaram quatro horas seguidas com o mesmo conteúdo na tela, com brilho, volume e resolução configurados da mesma forma.
O resultado mostrou uma vantagem considerável para o modelo maior. Enquanto o iPhone 18 Pro consumiu 15% da carga, o Pro Max gastou apenas 8% no mesmo período.
iPhone 18 Pro Max consome quase metade da bateria
Depois das quatro horas de reprodução, o iPhone 18 Pro Max gastou apenas 8% da carga, enquanto o iPhone 18 Pro consumiu 15% no mesmo período.
Isso equivale a uma média de consumo de 2% por hora no Pro Max e 3,75% por hora no Pro. A diferença de 7 pontos percentuais parece pequena à primeira vista, mas fica bem mais clara quando projetamos a autonomia total.
Caso esse ritmo permanecesse constante até a bateria chegar a 0%, o iPhone 18 Pro Max alcançaria cerca de 50 horas de reprodução contínua no YouTube.
Já o iPhone 18 Pro chegaria a aproximadamente 26 horas e 40 minutos. Na projeção, portanto, o Pro Max oferece cerca de 23 horas e 20 minutos a mais, ou uma autonomia aproximadamente 87,5% superior neste cenário específico.
O iPhone 18 Pro Max dura quase o dobro?
Neste teste, sim. O resultado mostra que o iPhone 18 Pro Max aproveita muito melhor a carga durante reprodução contínua de vídeos e chega perto de entregar o dobro da autonomia do iPhone 18 Pro.
É importante destacar que as 50 horas e 26h40 são estimativas matemáticas, não tempos medidos até o desligamento dos aparelhos. O consumo pode variar conforme a bateria se aproxima de 0%, além de fatores como temperatura e comportamento do sistema.
Ainda assim, como os celulares passaram exatamente pelo mesmo teste e sob as mesmas condições, o resultado deixa clara a vantagem do iPhone 18 Pro Max para quem prioriza bateria.
